extracted.intended_audience: poets and satirists (writers of Horatian/classical-style satire and polished verse)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for composing satire and poetic verse in the Horatian tradition: style, audience, ethical limits, revision, and rhetorical technique. Focuses on what makes satire effective (cadence, terseness, restraint) and what to avoid (malice, slovenly haste, inappropriate mixing of languages).

rubrics_metrics.name: quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not writing MUCH; writing WELL" — prefer careful, well-crafted verse to copious rapid output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticises poets who pour out verses quickly (e.g., Lucilius) leaving a "load of refuse" behind; readiness is not proof of power. Prioritise craftsmanship over sheer speed or volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: revise thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: "you must draw your pen not once nor twice but o'er and o'er again" — repeated revision is necessary to refine verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision (pruning redundancies, applying the file to excrescences) entices readers to return and elevates work beyond first drafts. Anti-pattern: publishing first-draft output after composing 'two hundred verses' without editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: maintain cadence and musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Strip what I write... of cadence and succession, time and note... no poetry you'll find" — rhythm and cadence are essential to making verse poetry rather than prose in metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic effects depend on ordered rhythm (time and note); removing metric cadence collapses verse into ordinary prose. Ensure lines have proper succession and musicality appropriate to poetic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: terse and clear expression
rubrics_metrics.description: "Terseness there wants, to make the thought ring clear, nor with a crowd of words confuse the ear" — favour concision so meaning rings clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid verbosity and 'windy nothings' that obscure sense. Use precise phrasing and economise words to avoid confusing the reader or dulling impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: plastic style and variety of tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a "plastic style, now grave, now light" — vary register and tone to suit subject and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good satiric style alternates seriousness and lightness; mimicry of oratorical or conversational registers as needed. Avoid monotonous one-register writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: mask strength; exercise restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: "Who masks his strength, and says not all he can" — the writer should often conceal full force of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraint (implication, suggestion) can be more powerful than explicit statement. Avoid saying everything bluntly; leave room for reader inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: use humour/pleasantry to cut through gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pleasantry will often cut clean through / Hard knots that gravity would scarce undo" — strategic levity can dissolve entrenched problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpose lightness or jest to make points more effective, particularly when dealing with heavy or knotty subjects. Use humour as a tool to reveal truth, not merely to entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: target a discerning audience, not the mob
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not making popular applause your cue, / But looking to fit audience, although few" — aim to please wise, discerning readers rather than seek mass vogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the approval of knowledgeable peers (Maecenas, Virgil, etc.) to the fickle laughter of crowds. Anti-pattern: courting a 'selfish laugh' or pandering for vogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid personal malice and slander
rubrics_metrics.description: "He who maligns an absent friend's fair fame..." — refrain from defaming absent persons or spreading lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'feign what he ne'er saw' or blab secrets for cheap laughs. Malicious detraction poisons social relations; satire should criticise vice, not engage in slander of private friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: proportion criticism and punishment to the offence
rubrics_metrics.description: "square her punishments to each offence" — reason should match punishment to the wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In satiric judgment, distinguish between slight faults and grave crimes; avoid treating all failings as equally heinous. Tone and severity should fit the scale of the target's misdeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: do not mistake rapid composition for superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness or speed (composing many lines quickly) is not proof of poetical strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage mocks those who boast of composing fastest (Crispinus' bet); value deliberation and refinement over feats of sheer speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: distinguish colloquial verse from true poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Colloquial verse a man may write like me, But (trust an author) 'tis not poetry... keep that name for genius" — simple metre without elevated substance is not full poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that metred conversation differs from high poetry; aspire to the richer, more sustained effects of 'genius' when the aim is genuine poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: mind linguistic register and appropriateness of mixed language
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning the "gift of mixing Latin up with Greek" — be careful when hybridizing registers or languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed-language flourishes can add grace but may be inappropriate for certain contexts (e.g., legal pleading). Choose linguistic mixtures only when they suit audience, purpose, and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: match style to medium (stage vs private recitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you "take away the rhythm, the self-same words / Would suit an angry father off the boards" — whether lines are for stage or for private reading affects their composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider performative needs (actors, buskins) versus the needs of a close literary audience; lines designed for recitation or stage may differ from polished written satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: portray vice boldly and concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Elder comic poets "portrayed [wrongdoers] without fear in strong relief" — vivid, fearless depiction of characters and vice is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong characterization and concrete detail to expose folly and vice. Bold depiction helps moral and comic impact, though it should not devolve into gratuitous malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: do not court applause by falsehood or fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: "Who courts a reckless laugh by random hits, / Who feigns what he ne'er saw, a secret blabs" — avoid inventing incidents just to win laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirists should not fabricate or exaggerate private matters merely to impress peers. Ethical limits and factual honesty maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: consider audience sensitivity and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: "satire finds small favour, since / Most men want whipping, and who want it, wince" — many readers dislike being mocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that audiences may bristle at satire; select subjects and modes of delivery that take readers' sensibilities and the context of reception into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance severity and mildness in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nor let you scourge when you should only cane... you're likely to be overmild" — calibrate tone between harshness and gentleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes: neither excessive cruelty nor pusillanimous mildness serves satire well. Choose corrective chastisement appropriate to the target and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: prune redundancies and excrescences in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: "He'd prune redundancies, apply the file / To each excrescence that deforms his style" — edit out excesses in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tidy diction by removing repetitive or superfluous phrasing; careful pruning sharpens effect and improves clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: use anecdotes and exempla for moral teaching, but ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator recounts parental exempla ('See the life that son of Albius leads!') as a method of warning youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ illustrative stories and examples to teach and persuade, but avoid using them as pretexts for gratuitous personal attacks or gossip.
